source.title: GPT-2's IOI behavior is defined where the paper's algorithm isn't

record.tranche_reason: The post tests the circuit account using a prompt manipulation and attention measurements, rather than the original circuit-discovery and patching method.
record.gate_note: The post reports matched-prompt behavioral results and attention patterns for named head classes. Descriptions of the original paper's algorithm and circuit are background, not new results. It reports no patching or logit decoding.
record.test_reason: The post runs a new prompt variant (the IO name incidentally duplicated in a modifier slot) on GPT-2. It measures IOI behaviour and the attention of the named head classes, and argues that the paper's 'remove duplicated names' algorithm does not predict the result. That is a result-based argument that V1's description needs restating, and a test of V6 on a new prompt format.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author concludes that DTH flagging a duplicate token is not, on its own, enough to substantially inhibit output of that token in IOI. GPT-2 still succeeds where the paper's stated algorithm is undefined. Without patching, the author does not say how this fits the S-Inhibition account and plans ablations next.
record.recipe_differences: The post varies prompts in matched pairs and measures behavior and per-head attention; it does not perform the original circuit decomposition or patching tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The incidental-duplicate modifier condition produces a small decrease in IO/S logit difference and accuracy relative to control.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative Name Mover heads shift attention toward the incidental IO duplicate much more than positive Name Movers do.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Negative name-mover heads respond differently from positive name movers to duplicated IO tokens.

record.problems: The post reports no patching or logit decoding, and says it has not determined how the findings fit the paper's account of S-Inhibition. It reports the head-attention results mostly qualitatively, without per-head numerical values. The experiment uses single-token names and one specific incidental-duplicate manipulation.

untested.parts: The full 26-head, 7-class circuit; faithfulness, completeness and minimality; causal roles of the heads (no patching or ablation).
All of it: no ablation of name movers, so no backup-head takeover is tested.
All of it: only GPT-2 (size not stated, presumably small), with no other models, checkpoints or tasks.
All of it: no alternative circuit-finding methods, ablation types or metrics.
All of it: no faithfulness or completeness evaluation under different ablations, metrics or distributions.
Name-order swaps, more names, other templates beyond the 8 used, and causal confirmation that the same components carry the variant.

record.verdict_notes: Model size is not stated ('GPT-2'); presumably GPT-2 small, the subject of the original paper. The control is described inconsistently: an unrelated name ('Cedar Park') in one place and a 'neutral non-name word' in another. The r3 measure wording ('attention back to the real IO') is taken from the post. All head-level results are attention patterns without causal tests, and per-head values are only in the linked notebook. This is a LessWrong post that has not been peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: It does not test the full 26-head, 7-class circuit, the faithfulness, completeness or minimality criteria, or the roles of all components by patching.
Backup-head takeover after ablating main name-mover heads is not tested.
Other models, sizes, checkpoints and component reuse on other tasks are not tested.
Alternative circuit-finding methods, ablation types and metrics are not compared.
The post varies the prompt condition, but does not compare ablation types or evaluation metrics, or test how much of IOI behavior the full circuit explains.
It tests a particular incidental-duplicate modification across 8 templates, but not different name orders, more names, or causal circuit identity across prompt variants.

rows.note: The author characterizes the effect as real but not large. The post does not give the control and test logit differences themselves.
rows.check: Drop V5: the row measures behaviour under a prompt variant, not how faithfulness or completeness scores depend on the ablation, metric or distribution. Against V1's algorithm, the predicted narrowing from the duplicate IO appears but is small (0.23, d = 0.27). Against V6, IOI holds with a small cost. Control and test logit differences themselves are not given.

rows.operation_detail: Observe S-Inhibition heads' attention in prompts with an incidental duplicate IO name

conditions.value: incidental duplicate IO name in modifier slot

rows.measure: Attention allocation between the S2 slot and the incidental duplicate
rows.value: Heads mostly continue attending to S2; one head does not shift, while two others shift toward the incidental duplicate but still substantially prefer S2 on average
rows.note: No per-head numerical values are provided. The author says the heads do not inhibit the incidental token as much as the simple duplicate-removal prediction would suggest.

statements.problem: The study measures S2-focused attention, not S2-focused inhibition. The wording turns an attention observation into a causal finding.
